sentences.text: NaNoGenMo, National Novel Generation Month, is an annual event in which participants spend November writing code that generates a novel of 50,000 words or more and, at the end, share at least one novel together with the source code that made it.

It is organised as a community on GitHub, one repository per edition, with its page at nanogenmo.github.io; as an event series its unit is a participant's issue on an edition's repository, carrying dev diaries, sample output, at least one generated novel and its source code.
What it holds is the record of code-generated novels of 50,000 words or more and their source code, shared by participants each November since 2013.
In its own words the event is "based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted on a whim"; it started in 2013 from that off-hand idea of the internet artist and programmer.

It takes its measure from National Novel Writing Month, "in the spirit of" that event's "interesting definition of a novel as 50,000 words of fiction", and stays a distinct event: one account calls it a spoof of National Novel Writing Month, and Liza Daly calls it a tongue-in-cheek competition that, like its inspiration, has no prizes or rankings.
The page states a single rule: "The only rule is that you share at least one novel and also your source code at the end."

Daly counts two rules, at least 50,000 words of output and the source code published, and another account has the community posting its generated novels and the code that produced them in the open on GitHub.
The activity runs from 12:01am GMT on 1 November to 12:01am GMT on 1 December; the code need not be on GitHub, where the repository serves to organise the community and its Issues work as a forum.

sentences.sense: what counts as a novel, and what it is made from
sentences.text: The novel is "defined however you want": the page offers "50,000 repetitions of the word "meow"" and a program that could "literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg", only the count of 50k+ words mattering.

sentences.sense: what counts as a novel, and what it is made from
sentences.text: A generated novel may thus be made from existing text, and the event points to such text: each edition has an open issue for resources (libraries, corpuses, APIs, techniques), the resource threads of old editions hold many more, and the page recommends corpora, a repository of public-domain lists of things.

sentences.sense: what counts as a novel, and what it is made from
sentences.text: The entries Daly singles out from 2017 show the range: Markov chains over a good corpus, text scraped from Wikipedia entries on mass shootings mixed with handwritten narrative, the source material of Tom Phillips' A Humument, Pride and Prejudice cut down by the organiser hugovk's transformations, books replaced sentence by sentence from other corpora by edit distance, word substitution by semantic relationship, and a neural network trained on crowd-sourced first sentences, with a warning about unsanitized input data.

sentences.sense: what counts as a novel, and what it is made from
sentences.text: Early entries used Markov chains, scraped text and procedural tricks; in later years participants increasingly reached for neural language models, which one account reads as an informal timeline of how machine text generation evolved.

On copyright the page asks and declines to enforce, "Please try to respect copyright. We're not going to police it", the responsibility resting "on your head", and the source code "does not have to be licensed in a particular way, so long as you share it."

A participant declares intent in an issue under their own GitHub account, and the saved page states no rule on how a generated novel is credited; crediting of the generated text and of any source it draws on is left to each participant, attribution practice varies across repositories, and a claim about an edition rests on its particular repositories.
In third-party accounts the entries stand under their makers' names: Eoin Noble, Janelle Shane, Nick Montfort, hugovk and Kevan Davis are among those Daly names for 2017.

A participant opens an issue on the edition's repository to declare the intent to participate, titles it by the kind of project, updates it through the month with dev diaries and sample output, and may comment on others' issues; the official admins, @dariusk and @hugovk, keep the issues organised and tagged.
Readback runs through each edition's repository issues, with a resources issue per edition, from 2013 to 2025; the census has left the edition repositories and their issues unread.
Thirteen editions are listed, 2013 to 2025, and the page as read on 1 November 2026, the first day of that year's period, lists no 2026 edition.

The GitHub organisation shows 61 followers; Daly counts a hundred or so participants each November and more than 100 other projects in 2017, with hundreds more from other years, and the record leaves the number of participants or novels in any edition unstated.
Its sister events are NaPoGenMo, National Poetry Generation Month, NaOpGenMo, National Opera Generation Month, and NaMoGenMo, National Movie Generation Month.

Daly reads the entries as tributes to human creativity, often deliberately bad or unreadable, and as a chance to write throwaway code in public, and finds that news stories asking "Can AIs Replace Authors?" miss the spirit of the endeavour; self-describing books are, in Daly's account, practically a sub-genre.

sentences.text: A Reddit answer reads the 50,000-word requirement as no strict literary goal, one that frees participants to reach the count through various means (its snippet breaks off at "unconve...").

CenterConsulting calls the spirit exploratory and often comic, the experiment being the point, and reads the event as a reminder that computers writing prose was a hobbyist curiosity before large language models made it a business question, its open code-sharing set against today's closed, monetized text generators.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: In the traininglayerliterature.org layer census it belongs to two areas, machine composition ("Reception becoming composition: readers, models and practices that make new writing from what they read") and field history, and stands to the census, whose question is how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus and what that apparatus makes from it, as an empirical comparator.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: The census's question for it is what a program makes into a novel of 50k+ words, from which sources, with code and output shared together.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: The archive reads it as an inspectable program/output community in the machine-composition direction: each novel is shared with its code under a participant's account, so what a program makes from its source texts, a Project Gutenberg novel or a pooled corpus, can be read beside the program that made it.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: Novels written by code fall in the column the archive's field survey calls writing through AI, where the machine is method or procedure; the procedural lineage, from the Oulipo through electronic literature to computational poetics, established that composition can be delegated to systems, the machine there being method and not yet addressee.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: The archive keeps that practice apart from training-layer literature, which has a human writer and a machine reader: AI-generated literature has the machine as writer, procedural or computational poetry has it as method, computational poetics analyzes text computationally where training-layer literature composes for computation, computational poetry is poetry generated by computational systems, and AI-generated content is writing whose author is a language model.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: By its own statement the event is no AI or LLM project: its rules name code, and the novel is defined however the participant wants.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: In the archive's field survey a road-trip novel written by a sensor-fed network established generation-at-scale as an artifact, and the texts of the practices with and through machines are in the corpora, read by machines incidentally.

sentences.text: Whether any generated novel or its source text is in a training corpus or a model is unrecorded; the record gives for the layer only the event's allowance of novels made from existing text and its pointer to public-domain corpora.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: Machine composition, in the archive's terms, is what an encountered work makes it possible for a machine to write, and a reception event may end in new writing: Virgil reads Homer and writes Virgil.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: Each output element is typed on four coordinates, among them source status (retrieved, generated, mixed, uncertain) and provenance status (marked, unmarked, misattributed, uncertain), so that whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from stay different questions.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: Uptake is not awarded on temporal succession, dependence on the encountered work having to be shown, and no claim is made about a composing system's interiority, transformation being measured on artifacts.

sentences.sense: machine composition and the training layer
sentences.text: The case the archive marks as especially important is recursive, an emitted artifact entering a later corpus and a later model: x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′.

NaNoGenMo is distinct from National Novel Writing Month, whose definition of a novel it borrows, and is no curated anthology, its only rule the sharing of a novel and its code; Wikipedia has no article under either of its names.

sentences.text: NaNoGenMo, National Novel Generation Month, is an activity in which participants spend November writing code that generates a novel of 50k+ words; it is based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted on a whim, and one account dates its start to 2013.
It follows National Novel Writing Month's definition of a novel as 50,000 words of fiction and is described as a spoof of that event and as a tongue-in-cheek competition with no prizes or rankings.

The only rule is to share at least one novel and the source code at the end; Liza Daly counts two rules, 50,000 words of output and the published source code, and the community posts novels and code in the open on GitHub.
The activity runs from 12:01am GMT on 1 November to 12:01am GMT on 1 December, and editions are listed from 2013 to 2025.

Participants open an issue on the edition's repository, title it by their project, post dev diaries and sample output and comment on others' issues; the admins are @dariusk and @hugovk, and GitHub's Issues serve as the forum, though the code need not be there.

The novel is defined however the participant wants, as 50,000 repetitions of "meow" or a random novel grabbed from Project Gutenberg; each edition has a resources issue for libraries, corpuses, APIs and techniques, and the page recommends the corpora repository of public-domain lists.
Copyright is a request the organisers do not police, and the code need not be licensed in any particular way.

Entries of 2017 used Markov chains over a corpus, text scraped from Wikipedia, the source material of A Humument, transformations of Pride and Prejudice, edit-distance replacement from other corpora, word substitution and a neural network trained on crowd-sourced sentences.
Early entries used Markov chains, scraped text and procedural tricks, later ones increasingly neural language models.
About a hundred people take part each November; more than 100 other projects were made in 2017, and the GitHub organisation has 61 followers.
Its sister events are NaPoGenMo, NaOpGenMo and NaMoGenMo.

Daly reads the entries as tributes to human creativity, often deliberately bad, and news coverage of AI replacing authors as missing their spirit, with self-describing books a sub-genre; a Reddit answer reads the word count as no strict literary goal; CenterConsulting calls the spirit exploratory and comic and sets its open code-sharing against closed, monetized generators.

L_BA.text: NaNoGenMo, National Novel Generation Month, is an annual event in which participants spend November writing code that generates a novel of 50,000 words or more and, at the end, share at least one novel together with the source code that made it. It is organised as a community on GitHub, one repository per edition, with its page at nanogenmo.github.io; as an event series its unit is a participant's issue on an edition's repository, carrying dev diaries, sample output, at least one generated novel and its source code. What it holds is the record of code-generated novels of 50,000 words or more and their source code, shared by participants each November since 2013. In its own words the event is "based on an idea Darius Kazemi tweeted on a whim"; it started in 2013 from that off-hand idea of the internet artist and programmer. It takes its measure from National Novel Writing Month, "in the spirit of" that event's "interesting definition of a novel as 50,000 words of fiction", and stays a distinct event: one account calls it a spoof of National Novel Writing Month, and Liza Daly calls it a tongue-in-cheek competition that, like its inspiration, has no prizes or rankings. The page states a single rule: "The only rule is that you share at least one novel and also your source code at the end." Daly counts two rules, at least 50,000 words of output and the source code published, and another account has the community posting its generated novels and the code that produced them in the open on GitHub. The activity runs from 12:01am GMT on 1 November to 12:01am GMT on 1 December; the code need not be on GitHub, where the repository serves to organise the community and its Issues work as a forum. The novel is "defined however you want": the page offers "50,000 repetitions of the word "meow"" and a program that could "literally grab a random novel from Project Gutenberg", only the count of 50k+ words mattering. A generated novel may thus be made from existing text, and the event points to such text: each edition has an open issue for resources (libraries, corpuses, APIs, techniques), the resource threads of old editions hold many more, and the page recommends corpora, a repository of public-domain lists of things. The entries Daly singles out from 2017 show the range: Markov chains over a good corpus, text scraped from Wikipedia entries on mass shootings mixed with handwritten narrative, the source material of Tom Phillips' A Humument, Pride and Prejudice cut down by the organiser hugovk's transformations, books replaced sentence by sentence from other corpora by edit distance, word substitution by semantic relationship, and a neural network trained on crowd-sourced first sentences, with a warning about unsanitized input data. Early entries used Markov chains, scraped text and procedural tricks; in later years participants increasingly reached for neural language models, which one account reads as an informal timeline of how machine text generation evolved. On copyright the page asks and declines to enforce, "Please try to respect copyright. We're not going to police it", the responsibility resting "on your head", and the source code "does not have to be licensed in a particular way, so long as you share it." A participant declares intent in an issue under their own GitHub account, and the saved page states no rule on how a generated novel is credited; crediting of the generated text and of any source it draws on is left to each participant, attribution practice varies across repositories, and a claim about an edition rests on its particular repositories. In third-party accounts the entries stand under their makers' names: Eoin Noble, Janelle Shane, Nick Montfort, hugovk and Kevan Davis are among those Daly names for 2017. A participant opens an issue on the edition's repository to declare the intent to participate, titles it by the kind of project, updates it through the month with dev diaries and sample output, and may comment on others' issues; the official admins, @dariusk and @hugovk, keep the issues organised and tagged. Readback runs through each edition's repository issues, with a resources issue per edition, from 2013 to 2025; the census has left the edition repositories and their issues unread. Thirteen editions are listed, 2013 to 2025, and the page as read on 1 November 2026, the first day of that year's period, lists no 2026 edition. The GitHub organisation shows 61 followers; Daly counts a hundred or so participants each November and more than 100 other projects in 2017, with hundreds more from other years, and the record leaves the number of participants or novels in any edition unstated. Its sister events are NaPoGenMo, National Poetry Generation Month, NaOpGenMo, National Opera Generation Month, and NaMoGenMo, National Movie Generation Month. Daly reads the entries as tributes to human creativity, often deliberately bad or unreadable, and as a chance to write throwaway code in public, and finds that news stories asking "Can AIs Replace Authors?" miss the spirit of the endeavour; self-describing books are, in Daly's account, practically a sub-genre. A Reddit answer reads the 50,000-word requirement as no strict literary goal, one that frees participants to reach the count through various means (its snippet breaks off at "unconve..."). CenterConsulting calls the spirit exploratory and often comic, the experiment being the point, and reads the event as a reminder that computers writing prose was a hobbyist curiosity before large language models made it a business question, its open code-sharing set against today's closed, monetized text generators. In the traininglayerliterature.org layer census it belongs to two areas, machine composition ("Reception becoming composition: readers, models and practices that make new writing from what they read") and field history, and stands to the census, whose question is how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus and what that apparatus makes from it, as an empirical comparator. The census's question for it is what a program makes into a novel of 50k+ words, from which sources, with code and output shared together. The archive reads it as an inspectable program/output community in the machine-composition direction: each novel is shared with its code under a participant's account, so what a program makes from its source texts, a Project Gutenberg novel or a pooled corpus, can be read beside the program that made it. Novels written by code fall in the column the archive's field survey calls writing through AI, where the machine is method or procedure; the procedural lineage, from the Oulipo through electronic literature to computational poetics, established that composition can be delegated to systems, the machine there being method and not yet addressee. The archive keeps that practice apart from training-layer literature, which has a human writer and a machine reader: AI-generated literature has the machine as writer, procedural or computational poetry has it as method, computational poetics analyzes text computationally where training-layer literature composes for computation, computational poetry is poetry generated by computational systems, and AI-generated content is writing whose author is a language model. By its own statement the event is no AI or LLM project: its rules name code, and the novel is defined however the participant wants. In the archive's field survey a road-trip novel written by a sensor-fed network established generation-at-scale as an artifact, and the texts of the practices with and through machines are in the corpora, read by machines incidentally. Whether any generated novel or its source text is in a training corpus or a model is unrecorded; the record gives for the layer only the event's allowance of novels made from existing text and its pointer to public-domain corpora. Machine composition, in the archive's terms, is what an encountered work makes it possible for a machine to write, and a reception event may end in new writing: Virgil reads Homer and writes Virgil. Each output element is typed on four coordinates, among them source status (retrieved, generated, mixed, uncertain) and provenance status (marked, unmarked, misattributed, uncertain), so that whether a machine wrote something new and whether it told the truth about where it came from stay different questions. Uptake is not awarded on temporal succession, dependence on the encountered work having to be shown, and no claim is made about a composing system's interiority, transformation being measured on artifacts. The case the archive marks as especially important is recursive, an emitted artifact entering a later corpus and a later model: x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′. NaNoGenMo is distinct from National Novel Writing Month, whose definition of a novel it borrows, and is no curated anthology, its only rule the sharing of a novel and its code; Wikipedia has no article under either of its names. Asked for the event by its acronym on 1 November 2026, the first day of its period, Google's AI Overview reached the event by name and gave its goal, period, rules, joining, origin and admins, mainly from its own page; the Capture Registry finds the period and the sharing rule composed exactly. The registry finds the novel taken whole from existing text absent, the page's examples replaced by a list of techniques, and the resources and corpora the page points to not carried, the closing offering generation techniques. It finds the copyright request, which the page asks and declines to enforce, given as a rule in force, and the statement that the code need not be licensed not carried. It records the admins' handles given as full names, Darius Kazemi's on the page and Hugo van Kemenade's on no saved page, no participant or novel named, no current edition named on the first day of the period, 'spoof' taken from the CenterConsulting card, the sister events not carried, no institution named, and the paste possibly truncated on a video card.
